title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one solution exists; you may not use the same element twice.
approach: One-pass hash map: for each number, check whether target minus it has already been seen; if so return both indices, otherwise record the number's index and move on.
trace_input: nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9 -> the answer should land on the second element so the map gets at least one entry first; if it resolves too early, use nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s: the same letters with the same counts, in any order.
approach: Single count array of 26 slots: increment for each character of s, decrement for each character of t, then the strings are anagrams iff every slot is zero.
trace_input: s = "race", t = "care" (visualize the count structure as a compact map of only nonzero letters, not 26 array cells)

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.
approach: Grow a hash set while scanning: if the current number is already in the set, return true immediately; otherwise add it.
trace_input: nums = [1, 3, 2, 3] -> returns true on the second 3

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements, in any order.
approach: Bucket sort by frequency: count occurrences in a hash map, place each number into a bucket indexed by its count, then walk buckets from highest count down collecting k elements.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given an integer array nums, return an array where each position holds the product of every element except the one at that position, without using division and in O(n).
approach: Two sweeps over an output array: a forward pass writes the running product of everything to the left, a backward pass multiplies in the running product of everything to the right.

title: Valid Sudoku
statement: Given a 9x9 Sudoku board (digits and empty cells), determine whether the filled cells are valid: no digit repeats in any row, column, or 3x3 box.
approach: One scan with hash sets keyed by (row, digit), (column, digit), and (box, digit): a repeat key means invalid. Visualize a small 4x4 analogue or a partial board so state stays readable.
trace_input: a 4-row partial board where row 0 = [5, 3, ., .], row 1 = [6, ., ., 5], row 2 = [., 5, ., .], and the second 5 in column-check or box-check produces the interesting collision; keep structures to the three sets plus the scanned cells

title: Encode and Decode Strings
statement: Design encode(list of strings) -> single string and decode(string) -> original list, robust to any characters including delimiters appearing inside the strings.
approach: Length prefixing: encode each string as <length>#<string>; decode by reading digits up to '#', then consuming exactly that many characters. No escaping needed because the length says where the string ends.
trace_input: ["neet", "co#de"] -> encoded "4#neet5#co#de" -> decoded back; the '#' inside co#de is the teaching moment

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers, in O(n).
approach: Hash set of all numbers; only a number with no left neighbor (num - 1 absent) starts a sequence, then count upward while num + 1 exists. Each number is visited at most twice.
